document.sourceText: Nec ego ipse capio totum quod sum. Ergo animus ad habendum se ipsum angustus est, ut ubi sit quod sui non capit? Numquid extra ipsum ac non in ipso? Quomodo ergo non capit? Multa mihi super hoc oboritur admiratio, stupor apprehendit me. Et eunt homines mirari alta montium et ingentes fluctus maris et latissimos lapsus fluminum et Oceani ambitum et gyros siderum, et relinquunt se ipsos, nec mirantur quod haec omnia, cum dicerem, non ea videbam oculis, nec tamen dicerem, nisi montes et fluctus et flumina et sidera quae vidi et Oceanum quem credidi intus in memoria mea viderem, spatiis tam ingentibus quasi foris viderem.

analysis.sourceText: Nec ego ipse capio totum quod sum. Ergo animus ad habendum se ipsum angustus est, ut ubi sit quod sui non capit? Numquid extra ipsum ac non in ipso? Quomodo ergo non capit? Multa mihi super hoc oboritur admiratio, stupor apprehendit me. Et eunt homines mirari alta montium et ingentes fluctus maris et latissimos lapsus fluminum et Oceani ambitum et gyros siderum, et relinquunt se ipsos, nec mirantur quod haec omnia, cum dicerem, non ea videbam oculis, nec tamen dicerem, nisi montes et fluctus et flumina et sidera quae vidi et Oceanum quem credidi intus in memoria mea viderem, spatiis tam ingentibus quasi foris viderem.
analysis.literalTranslation: Nor do I myself comprehend the whole of what I am. Therefore the mind is too narrow for holding itself, so that where is that which it does not contain of itself? Surely it is outside itself and not in itself? How then does it not contain it? Great wonder arises in me concerning this; amazement seizes me. And people go to marvel at the heights of mountains and the mighty waves of the sea and the very broad courses of rivers and the circuit of Ocean and the revolutions of the stars, and they leave themselves behind, nor do they marvel that all these things, when I spoke of them, I was not seeing with my eyes; and yet I would not speak of them unless I were seeing within, in my memory, the mountains and waves and rivers and stars which I saw, and the Ocean which I believed, in spaces so vast as though I were seeing them outside.
analysis.naturalTranslation: Nor do I myself comprehend all that I am. The mind, then, is too narrow to contain itself. Where, then, is that part of itself which it cannot contain? Surely it cannot be outside itself and not within itself. How, then, can it fail to contain it? Great wonder at this rises within me; I am seized with astonishment. People go out to marvel at mountain heights, the huge waves of the sea, the broad courses of rivers, the sweep of Ocean, and the revolutions of the stars, yet they leave themselves behind. They do not marvel that, when I spoke of all these things, I was not seeing them with my eyes; and yet I could not have spoken of them unless inwardly, in my memory, I saw the mountains, waves, rivers, and stars I had seen, and the Ocean whose existence I believed, spread through spaces as vast as though I were seeing them outside myself.

notes.text: The repeated verb capio develops a deliberate semantic tension between intellectual comprehension and spatial containment: the speaker cannot fully comprehend himself, while the mind cannot fully contain itself.
Habendum is a gerund governed by ad; se ipsum remains its direct object, so the construction is not a gerundive agreeing with an expressed noun.
The sequence ut ubi sit is rhetorically compressed: ut presents the consequence of the mind's narrowness, while ubi introduces the question of where the uncontained part could be.
Quod is accusative as the object of capit within the free relative expression quod sui non capit; sui is a reflexive genitive referring back to animus.
With the sense 'concerning' or 'about,' super governs the ablative in prose; hoc is therefore analyzed as ablative here.
The deponent infinitive mirari complements eunt and expresses the activity toward which the movement is directed: people 'go to marvel at' these sights.
Quod is declarative rather than relative here, introducing the content at which the people fail to marvel.
Haec omnia is fronted before the cum-clause and is naturally construed as the object of dicerem; ea then resumes the same referents as the object of videbam.
The imperfect subjunctive dicerem forms the apodosis associated with the nisi-clause whose verb is viderem, giving the sense 'I would not speak' or, in context, 'I could not have spoken.'
In Oceanum quem credidi, the relative expression is elliptical: the sense is that the speaker believed the Ocean to exist or accepted its reality without having seen it directly.
Spatiis tam ingentibus is an ablative phrase describing the vast spatial dimensions under which the remembered images are represented internally.
Quasi introduces a hypothetical comparison with the imperfect subjunctive viderem: the inward images appear as though they were being seen externally.
